title: Accessible Computer Science for K-12 Students with Hearing Impairments
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to make K-12 computer science instruction more accessible for Deaf and Hard of Hearing (D/HH) students, especially those with hearing impairments and limited access to computer science resources in American Sign Language (ASL). The authors argue that many existing captions and text-based explanations are too difficult or linguistically mismatched for some D/HH learners, and that accessible programming instruction should better align with Deaf culture, ASL, and visual learning preferences.

The paper presents an early-stage project design for an accessible block-based computer science curriculum and web application. The intervention concept includes ASL video explanations of core programming topics, captions, and accessibility features such as visual feedback, ASL tooltips for blocks, adjustable video speed, and user choice between ASL and text tooltips. It also describes a companion robot-based programming environment intended to support hands-on learning.

The intended population is middle-school D/HH students within a broader K-12 accessible computing initiative, along with teachers and sign language experts who may use the materials in classrooms. The paper is primarily a design and position paper rather than an evaluation study; it reports no outcome data from student use. Its main conclusion is that ASL-centered, multimodal accessibility features are needed and promising for D/HH students, and that future work will test the impact of these videos and tools with middle-school deaf learners.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI/chatbot system that produces text and instructional content; no specific commercial or research product is named in the paper.
identified_tools.use_case: Not actually studied as an AI literacy intervention. The paper is a conceptual/design paper about accessible block-based K-12 computer science resources for Deaf/Hard of Hearing students, including ASL videos and accessibility features.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/future-work paper with no empirical comparison groups, no outcome data, and no evaluated AI literacy intervention. The paper proposes accessibility supports for K-12 CS learning rather than reporting study results.
impact_tier_rationale: No measured effect on reading, literacy, or subgroup outcomes is reported. Claims about Deaf/Hard of Hearing learners, post-lingual vs. pre-lingual students, and accessibility benefits are speculative or design-oriented rather than evidence of impact.
